implementation_notes: The classic Interceptor/InvocationContext structure collapses into a decorator: a closure receives the callable, records the attempt, calls it, records the outcome and re-raises, with functools.wraps preserving the wrapped function's metadata. It is the default for application-level auditing because it needs nothing beyond the standard library and the audit policy stays visible at the definition site; its limit is that it only covers the decorated name.
pitfalls: A decorator only wraps the decorated name: aliases taken before decoration, bound methods looked up on the class and self-calls are not audited.
An exception raised while writing the audit record propagates into the business call path - decide fail-open versus fail-closed deliberately.
functools.wraps sets __wrapped__, so frameworks that follow it (inspect.signature, some DI containers) still see the original function - the wrapper hides nothing from them.

variants.name: CPython runtime audit hooks (PEP 578)
variants.implementation_notes: PEP 578 installs audit hooks in the interpreter: sys.addaudithook(callback) receives every raised audit event (open, socket.connect, subprocess.Popen, import, exec and many more) as (event, args) before the operation completes, which is interception below the application layer that the audited code cannot remove once the hook is installed. Use it for security events inside the runtime and for tooling around untrusted code - not as a sandbox (the PEP says so explicitly) and not as a replacement for application-level interception, because plain method calls never raise audit events.
pitfalls: Audit hooks cannot be removed or unregistered once added, and an exception raised inside a hook aborts the audited operation - keep the hook fast and total.
Hooks are called for every raised event, including events raised while the hook itself runs: recursive logging must be guarded or the process floods.
Only events the runtime raises are seen; ordinary method calls, attribute access and C-extension internals produce no audit event at all, so the hook is not complete mediation.
